title: Psychosis and schizophrenia
blurb: Recognise positive and negative symptoms, explain the causes, and apply NICE CG178 from early intervention to recovery.
question: Tyler, 19, has become withdrawn over 6 months, stopped attending college, and now says neighbours are talking about him through the walls. His GP refers him. Which service and treatment package does NICE recommend?

teach.body: Psychosis is a state in which a person's perception and beliefs lose contact with shared reality: hallucinations, delusions and disorganised thinking. Schizophrenia is the most common long-term psychotic illness. In plain English: the brain is producing experiences that feel completely real to the person but are not shared by others. It is treatable, and many people recover well, especially with early help.

rows.label: Response
values: Harder to treat; arts therapies may help

teach.caption: No single gene causes schizophrenia; combinations of genes raise vulnerability, and stressful events or drugs can trigger an episode (NHS, Causes of schizophrenia).
Even identical twins are not always both affected, so genes are not the only factor.

teach.body: EIP services should be open to everyone with a first episode or first presentation of psychosis, whatever their age or how long the psychosis has gone untreated. Assess without delay; if EIP cannot respond to a crisis, refer to a crisis resolution and home treatment team. EIP offers medication, psychological, social, occupational and educational help, and can extend beyond 3 years if recovery is not stable.

head: Intervention
Key detail
rows: Chosen together; not started in primary care without a consultant psychiatrist
At least 10 planned sessions over 3–12 months
Education and support programme as early as possible
teach.caption: CG178 1.3.4.1, 1.3.2.1, 1.3.7, 1.1.4, 1.4.4.3, 1.5.8.1.

root.label: Distress, falling function, plus attenuated symptoms or first-degree relative
root.sub: Refer without delay to specialist or EIP service

teach.body: Tyler is referred to the EIP team, who assess him within days. Care coordinator Nurse Mensah builds trust, explores his beliefs without arguing, and involves his mother with his agreement. He is offered an oral antipsychotic chosen with him, individual CBTp and family intervention, plus help returning to college. She asks about cannabis use non-judgementally and starts baseline physical health checks.

teach.text: Negative symptoms are easily mistaken for laziness, depression or medication sedation. And a person at risk of psychosis (attenuated symptoms, no established psychosis) should be offered CBT, not antipsychotics.

items: Positive: hallucinations, delusions, thought disorder. Negative: alogia, avolition, anhedonia, blunted affect, withdrawal.
Stress-vulnerability: genes and development raise risk; stress and drugs such as cannabis trigger episodes.
EIP for any first episode, any age, any duration of untreated psychosis; assess without delay.
First episode: oral antipsychotic plus CBTp (16+ sessions) and family intervention (10+).
At-risk mental state: CBT, not antipsychotics; crisis teams first line for acute community episodes.

summary: You can now distinguish positive and negative symptoms and explain psychosis through the stress-vulnerability model. You can apply NICE CG178 from early intervention through to recovery-focused care.

A.q: Which of the following is a negative symptom of schizophrenia?
options: Loss of motivation to start tasks
Hearing a voice commenting on actions
A belief of being followed by police
Speech that jumps between topics
A.why: Avolition (loss of motivation) is a negative symptom: something taken away from usual functioning.

whyNot.3: Thought disorder is classed with positive symptoms.

A.q: Who should have access to early intervention in psychosis services, according to NICE?
options: People aged 14 to 35 with a first episode
Anyone with a first episode, whatever their age
People untreated for less than 3 months
People who have already tried two antipsychotics
A.why: CG178 1.3.1.1: EIP should be accessible to all people with a first episode or first presentation of psychosis, irrespective of age or duration of untreated psychosis.

whyNot.0: NICE sets no age band for EIP access.
whyNot.2: Duration of untreated psychosis is not a barrier to EIP.
whyNot.3: Treatment resistance describes clozapine eligibility, not EIP.

A.q: How many planned sessions of individual CBT for psychosis does NICE recommend as a minimum?
A.why: CG178 1.3.7.1: CBTp is delivered one-to-one over at least 16 planned sessions.

whyNot.0: Six sessions is below the NICE minimum.
whyNot.1: Ten sessions is the minimum for family intervention, not CBTp.
whyNot.2: Twelve sessions is below the NICE minimum for CBTp.

B.q: Aisha, 22, is distressed and struggling at university. She has brief odd perceptual experiences and her mother has schizophrenia. She is not psychotic. What does NICE recommend?
options: Start a low-dose antipsychotic to prevent psychosis
Refer her without delay for specialist assessment
Reassure her and review in 12 months
Advise her to avoid stress until she graduates
B.why: CG178 1.2.1.1: distress, declining functioning and attenuated symptoms or a first-degree relative with psychosis means referral without delay to a specialist or EIP service. CBT is offered; antipsychotics are not (1.2.3).

whyNot.0: CG178 1.2.3.2: do not offer antipsychotics to people at increased risk.
whyNot.2: Waiting a year ignores a recognised at-risk presentation.
whyNot.3: Advice alone does not meet the referral recommendation.

B.q: Ben, 28, with schizophrenia, has persistent negative symptoms after his positive symptoms improved. Which intervention does NICE suggest considering, particularly for negative symptoms?
options: Arts therapies
Supportive counselling
Benzodiazepines
Adherence therapy
B.why: CG178 1.4.4.3 and 1.5.4.4: consider arts therapies for all people with psychosis, particularly to alleviate negative symptoms.

whyNot.1: CG178 says do not routinely offer counselling and supportive psychotherapy as specific interventions.
whyNot.2: Benzodiazepines do not treat negative symptoms.
whyNot.3: CG178 1.4.4.7 says do not offer adherence therapy as a specific intervention.

B.q: Kemi, 30, with schizophrenia, wants to stop smoking. Which statement about support is correct?
options: Offer bupropion as the first-choice aid
Delay quitting until her psychosis has gone
Offer help, noting drug levels may change
Advise cutting down rather than stopping
B.why: CG178 1.1.2.3-1.1.2.4: offer help to stop smoking even if previous attempts failed, being aware that reducing smoking can change the metabolism of drugs such as clozapine and olanzapine. Do not offer bupropion to people with psychosis.

whyNot.0: NICE advises not offering bupropion to people with psychosis to stop smoking.
whyNot.1: Support should not be withheld until psychosis resolves.
whyNot.3: NICE supports stopping, with attention to medication levels.

C.q: Eddie, 45, has schizophrenia and an acute relapse at home. The risk is now more than his community team can manage, but he is eating and sleeping, does not want admission and could be supported with daily visits. Which service is first line?
options: Immediate admission under section 2
A routine outpatient clinic in 6 weeks
Crisis resolution and home treatment
Weekly visits from his care coordinator
C.why: CG178 1.4.1.1: offer crisis resolution and home treatment teams as the first-line service during an acute episode in the community when its severity or risk exceeds what other community teams can manage; CG178 1.4.1.3: consider acute community treatment by these teams before admission.

whyNot.0: Detention is not indicated when risk can be managed at home.
whyNot.1: A 6-week wait is far too slow for an acute relapse with raised risk.
whyNot.3: The stem says the risk already exceeds what his community team can manage, so routine weekly visits are not enough.

C.q: Liam, 24, has had two episodes of psychosis and uses cannabis daily. His mother asks whether cannabis could be making things worse. What is the most accurate answer?
options: Cannabis use can trigger relapse or slow recovery
Cannabis is the single cause of his schizophrenia
Cannabis has a calming effect that protects him
Cannabis matters before a first episode, not after
C.why: NHS: drug use, particularly cannabis, increases the risk of psychosis, and in people who have had psychosis it can cause relapse or stop symptoms improving.

whyNot.1: No single factor causes schizophrenia; it arises from vulnerability plus triggers.
whyNot.2: Cannabis raises, not lowers, psychosis risk.
whyNot.3: Continued use after an episode can cause relapse.

C.q: Nina, 33, has schizophrenia that has not responded to adequate trials of risperidone and then olanzapine, each at optimum dose for 6 weeks with good adherence. What does NICE recommend next?
options: Try a third non-clozapine antipsychotic
Combine risperidone and olanzapine
Stop medication and offer CBTp instead
Offer clozapine
C.why: CG178 1.5.7.2: offer clozapine to people whose illness has not responded to adequate doses of at least 2 antipsychotics, at least one a non-clozapine second-generation drug.

whyNot.0: After two adequate trials, NICE recommends clozapine, not a third drug.
whyNot.1: Combining antipsychotics is not the NICE step for treatment resistance.
whyNot.2: Stopping medication is not the recommended response to resistance.

reteach.title: Vulnerability plus triggers
reteach.question: How do you explain psychosis and its treatment simply?

blocks.body: Genes and early development fill a person's 'vulnerability bucket'. Stress, cannabis and other drugs add more. When it overflows, an episode happens. Treatment lowers the level (medication) and builds coping and support (CBTp, family intervention), so the bucket overflows less often.

blocks.text: At-risk but not psychotic: offer CBT, not antipsychotics.

explain.body: Positive: hallucinations, delusions, thought disorder. Negative: alogia (poverty of speech), avolition, anhedonia, blunted affect, social withdrawal.

options: Loss of pleasure in activities
Poverty of speech
A false fixed belief
Lack of emotional expression
test.why: Alogia is poverty of speech, a negative symptom.

explain.body: No single gene; combinations raise vulnerability. Identical twin: about 1 in 2 chance; non-identical twin: about 1 in 8; general population about 1 in 100. Stressful events and drugs, especially cannabis, can trigger episodes.

test.q: If one identical twin develops schizophrenia, what is the other twin's approximate chance of developing it?
options: 1 in 8
1 in 2
Nearly certain
test.why: NHS: in identical twins, if one develops schizophrenia the other has about a 1 in 2 chance, showing genes matter but are not the only factor.

whyNot.0: This is the general population chance.
whyNot.1: This is the figure for non-identical twins.
whyNot.3: It is about 1 in 2, so environment also matters.

explain.body: CBTp: one-to-one, at least 16 planned sessions. Family intervention: at least 10 planned sessions over 3 to 12 months, including the person where practical. Carers get education and support early.

test.q: Over what period should family intervention for psychosis usually be delivered?
options: 1 to 2 weeks
3 to 12 months
2 to 3 years
4 to 12 weeks
test.why: CG178 1.3.7.2: family intervention includes at least 10 planned sessions over 3 to 12 months.

whyNot.0: This is too short for 10 planned sessions.
whyNot.2: This is longer than NICE describes.
whyNot.3: This is shorter than NICE describes.

explain.body: Before calling it resistant: review diagnosis, adherence, dose and duration, psychological treatments and substance use. Then offer clozapine after adequate trials of at least 2 antipsychotics, one a non-clozapine second-generation drug.

test.q: Before deciding schizophrenia is treatment-resistant, what should the team check first?
options: That the person has had a course of ECT
That a depot has been offered and refused
That the person is detained under the MHA
That doses were adequate and taken
test.why: CG178 1.5.7.1: review the diagnosis and establish adherence at an adequate dose and duration, as well as psychological treatments and substance use.

whyNot.1: Depot refusal is not part of the definition.
whyNot.2: Legal status is not relevant to resistance.
